title: Bidirectional Dijkstra in London: Scale Routing ⚡
description: Watch how Bidirectional Dijkstra cuts search work by expanding from both start and target until the frontiers meet. This visualization shows why modern route planning engines can stay fast even as graphs grow massive.
ig_caption:
Bidirectional Dijkstra: How Modern Route Planners Scale — Inside high-scale navigation engines: Bidirectional Dijkstra visualised ⚡

Here’s the key idea (on a live city grid):
• Forward search starts at the start node
• Backward search starts at the goal node
• Both use Dijkstra’s priority rules
• When the two visited frontiers meet, you stitch the best route together

Why it scales:
On big maps, single-source Dijkstra can explore tons of nodes. Bidirectional search often reduces the explored area dramatically, so shortest path at scale becomes practical for real-time software engineering.

Takeaway: treat route planning like a two-front race—fewer expansions, same optimal path.

Debate question: should route planners always use bidirectional search, or are there cases where plain Dijkstra still wins?
